saints.name: Syncletica of Alexandria

summary.text: Syncletica, also rendered Synkletika, is remembered as an ascetic woman of Alexandria. The published account describes her distribution of inherited wealth, withdrawal with her sister, and instruction of women who gathered around her. It places her death around 350. The profile preserves the uncertainty of that dating and identifies the narrative as an ecclesiastical life.

blocks.text: The Alexandrian Life places Syncletica in a wealthy family. It associates her renunciation of marriage and inheritance with the death of her parents, care for her sister, and withdrawal into a crypt.

blocks.text: Syncletica was born at Alexandria, of wealthy parents, of Macedonian extraction, who had settled there. Being very beautiful and well-dowered, she was sought in marriage by many suitors; but declined all offers, for her girlish heart had awakened to a love truer and deeper than any human affection; the best of her love she gave to God, and she desired to be His, and His alone. On the death of her parents she devoted her attention to her blind sister; and together, they served God in prayer and almsgiving. In token of renunciation of the world, and to deliver herself from troublesome pursuit by fortune-hunters, she cut off her hair, and disposed of her estates, but she sought to avoid notice in all that she did, and to conceal her good deeds and self-sacrifices. Nevertheless, she became known, and young maidens and women resorted to her for advice, and to study her example. She was reluctant to be forced thus into a position which she dreaded; nevertheless, unable to refuse the girls and young women that assistance they so much needed, she gave them much instruction, which has been preserved to us in the record we have of her life, and her words abound in practical common sense.

blocks.text: GOARCH calls her an Amma, a female counterpart to an Abba, and presents her as a teacher of nuns. It repeats a tradition identifying her with a woman who sheltered Athanasius and notes the attribution of her Life to him. Those identifications should remain attributed traditions: the historical January source itself warns that the attribution to Athanasius is insufficiently established. Her surviving literary memory therefore includes both sayings and a biographical tradition whose authorship requires care.
